title: Zoom Grid
description: Lift one part off the strip, split it into ten again, and again, and watch the places being made.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit. With navDots the dots are controls in AI mode too: a tap on a dot starts that phase.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; Hint, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 640. One rounded card holding the key at its top right (Answer, Close, Enter, Next, or the Yes / No keys; no question bar), the working area (the whole card until Answer is tapped) and the answer drawer that slides in from the right; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 652 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it (y 656 to 892, the question and every line, printed), one small dot per phase at the right.

zones.layout: board, key only: no question bar, only its key at the right end of the top row (the question is on the bubble); the working area is the whole card (64, 108, 1472 x 520) until the child taps Answer, when the answer drawer (as tall as the working area, the key on its top row reading Close) slides in from the right
zones.controls: circles r 28 at cx 1388, 1460, 1532, cy 40: Hint (data-control again), sound, restart; 72-unit finger boxes
zones.dots: one small dot per phase at the footer's right (72-unit finger boxes, centred on the bubble), no text; in user AND AI mode each is a button (data-control phase-dot, data-phase k) that starts its phase

stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: Take one tenth off the strip, split it into ten, and find out what the next two places are called and where they came from.
writeup.look: A strip of ten on the left, a magnifier on the right holding the piece being split, and a name ladder running down the side.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Zoom Grid' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the splits made against the splits this phase lays out, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each new name lands on the ladder or each amount is written, and the second fixed at what this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The strip lies across the top left of the working area, 420 by 110 at 64,230, cut into ten pieces of 42 each, touching along their edges, shaded in amber where a tenth is being talked about. Lift a part takes one piece off the strip and carries it into the glass, and the place it came from stays drawn as a plain outlined gap along the strip, never closed up, so that the piece in the glass can be held against the hole it left. The glass is a round magnifier 300 across at 520,240, drawn with a plain rim and nothing written on it. Split by ten cuts whatever is in the glass into ten equal pieces along its length, and those pieces can be dragged back out one at a time and laid along the piece they came from, where exactly ten of them fill it and the tenth one closes it. Build the grid lays the hundred pieces of the whole out as a ten by ten grid, 400 by 400 at 500,240, one cell 40 by 40, every cell the same size and none overlapping; a cell shaded on the grid is rose, because a cell of this grid stands for hundredths, and a whole row shaded by dragging is the same rose. The third split is made on a single lifted cell and its ten pieces are drawn in sky blue inside the glass alone, because a thousand pieces of the whole are never drawn on this stage and the ladder carries that name instead. The name ladder runs down the right of the working area, 280 by 500 at 870,212, three rungs one under the other, each taking the name of a place as it is made together with its tie to the place above it, written in as the split finishes rather than printed in advance. The two writing slots stand at 64,480 and 64,570, each 380 by 80, one taking the amount as a fraction and one taking it with a point. The words bay runs along the foot of the working area, 800 by 90 at 64,640: an amount said in words lies along it with its last word lit, because that word names the denominator, and the boxes of a decimal fraction are drawn above it to be filled bottom first. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a count or an amount is asked for, with a fraction key beside them that draws a bar and opens a box above and a box below, and under those the word pad carrying this chapter's eight highlighted terms, place value, decimal place, decimal, decimal fraction, decimal point, tenths, hundredths and thousandths, turned towards a partner for the quiz and answered by press. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a digit standing to the left of the point is deep blue, a digit standing to the right of it is green, and the point itself is vermilion between them on every phase without exception, because a chapter whose whole subject is one dot cannot afford a frame where the dot has to be hunted for. A part standing for tenths is amber, one standing for hundredths is rose, one standing for thousandths is sky blue, and a zero that is only holding a place open is grey, whether it was written in on the left of a short numerator or printed on the end of a measurement. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome, and every one of the readings survives with the colour taken away, because a place is told by the heading written over it before it is ever told by a colour, a filling zero is told by the short arrow running inward from the point, and a zero printed on the end is told by the place counter that lights it. Grey never means faint: such a zero is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. A piece lifted into the glass is drawn larger than it is, and the stage says so: the rim carries a plain magnifier mark, the strip and the gap it left stay on the stage at their real size the whole time it is being cut, and the piece is walked back down to its own size before it is put back. Nothing else on this stage is ever drawn at a size it is not.
writeup.finish: The card shows the ladder the child built, the three names on it with their ties, and the last grid they shaded standing beside it.

phases.win: ten pieces fill the magnifier and the ladder writes that one tenth is ten hundredths
phases.does: splits the lifted piece into ten and counts the pieces back into the tenth
phases.goal: a hundredth is one tenth split into ten, so a tenth is ten hundredths
phases.says: Cut that one tenth into ten. How many of these make the tenth again?
phases.check: Away from the screen: cut one tenth of a strip into ten. How many of the new pieces would cover the whole strip?
phases.feels: the small pieces fill the piece they came out of, and there are nine more pieces of the strip still to go
phases.hands: Cut a strip into ten and keep the strip on the desk. Take one piece off it, cut that piece into ten, and lay the small pieces back along the space the tenth came out of, counting aloud as they go in. Do not clear the first strip away at any point. Then ask how many of the small pieces would cover the whole strip, and let the class work it out from the ten that filled one piece.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what was in the glass before it was cut? Second rung, the phase's: how many pieces did that one piece become? Third rung: the ten pieces walk back into the gap one at a time with the count spoken. The word pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: every number word met so far has meant more of something when it got bigger, and nothing in the two words says that the number underneath is counting how many pieces the whole was cut into.
wrong.move: says a hundredth must be bigger than a tenth, because a hundred is a bigger number than ten.
wrong.screen: one tenth and one hundredth are laid on the stage side by side at their real sizes, the tenth from the strip and the hundredth from the glass, with the small one standing on top of the large one so the ten that fit can be counted. The child's answer stays in the slot, and the ladder writes the tie between the two places on its own rung without a word being said about which answer was given.

wrong.why: ten pieces have just been counted out and the whole strip was ten pieces too, so the same count is easy to hang on the wrong thing.
wrong.move: counts the ten small pieces as making the whole strip, not the one piece they came out of.
wrong.screen: the ten small pieces walk back to their real size and lay themselves along the gap in the strip, where they fill one piece and go no further, and the other nine pieces of the strip stay drawn beside them untouched. The whole strip is then counted along its length as ten pieces of ten, and the count is written on the ladder as it finishes.

phases.screen: the strip of ten with one piece lifted and waiting in the magnifier
phases.soWhat: A hundredth is one tenth split into ten, so one tenth is ten hundredths.

phases.win: the third name lands on the ladder with its tie to the place above it
phases.does: splits it again and says what the new piece will be called before the ladder writes it
phases.goal: a thousandth is one hundredth split into ten, and the pattern carries on
phases.says: Split it once more. What do you think this one will be called?
phases.check: One hundredth is cut into ten. What is one piece called, and how many of them make one hundredth?
phases.feels: the same cut a third time, and the name could be said before the pieces were seen
phases.hands: With the strip and the hundred grid both still on the desk, take one cell of the grid and cut it into ten. Before the cutting, ask the class to write down what they think the new piece will be called and why. Then compare the guesses with what they get, and ask what the next name after that one would have to be, without drawing anything.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what was in the glass this time? Second rung, the phase's: what happened to the piece before this one when it was cut? Third rung: the ladder is cut back to its first two rungs and the child reads the tie between them aloud before the third cut runs. The word pad stays open.

wrong.why: each of the first two names arrived with a page of its own, so a third one looks as though it must come with something new attached.
wrong.move: waits for a new rule, because a third name feels like a third thing to learn rather than the same cut made again.
wrong.screen: the ladder is walked from the top with each rung read out as the split that made it, and the same split control that made the second name is the one that makes the third. The child's answer stays in the slot and the glass replays both cuts one after the other with nothing else on the stage moving.

wrong.why: the pieces were counted out of a hundredth and there were ten of them, and both of those words are true about what just happened.
wrong.move: names the new piece a ten hundredth, joining the count of pieces to the name of the piece they came from.
wrong.screen: the ten new pieces are counted back into the hundredth they came out of, and then the whole is counted along the ladder rung by rung: ten tenths, a hundred hundredths, and a thousand of these. The name lands on the ladder from that count, and the child's name stays written beside it on the same rung so the two can be read together.

phases.screen: a single cell of the hundred grid lifted into the magnifier
phases.soWhat: A thousandth is one hundredth split into ten, and every place is a tenth of the place on its left.
phases.concept: One more split, and the pattern is clear

phases.win: both slots fill and the shaded cells light in tens as the count is read back
phases.does: counts the shaded cells, writes the fraction, then writes the decimal
phases.goal: a shaded figure is read by counting the shaded parts and the total parts
phases.says: Count what is shaded. Now count the whole thing. Write both of them.
phases.check: A hundred grid has forty-three squares shaded. Write that as a fraction and as a decimal, and say where each number came from.
phases.feels: the bottom number is the whole grid and the top number is what is coloured, and counting in tens keeps both of them
phases.hands: Hand out printed ten by ten grids and call out a decimal such as zero point four seven. Each child shades that many squares, counting in rows of ten rather than one square at a time. Then let them swap grids and write down what their partner shaded, as a fraction first and then with a point. Ask what happens to the picture when the digit in the tenths place goes up by one, and how many squares that is.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many squares is the whole grid? Second rung, the phase's: how many of them are coloured? Third rung: the grid is cut to a single row of ten and the child reads that off into both slots. The number pad and the fraction key stay open.

wrong.why: ten is the number the eye lands on first in a ten by ten grid, and the last figure the class read off was a strip of ten.
wrong.move: counts the shaded squares and writes them over ten, because the grid has ten rows.
wrong.screen: the whole grid is counted out in rows of ten with the running count climbing at the top left until it reaches a hundred, and the count stays written under the grid. The child's fraction stays in its slot, a strip of ten is drawn beside the grid with the child's fraction shaded on it, and the two pictures stand together with plainly different amounts coloured in.

wrong.why: a hundred squares is a long way to count singly, and a count that has been started over twice does not feel like something to rely on.
wrong.move: counts the shaded squares one at a time and loses the place, then distrusts a count that was right.
wrong.screen: the grid is counted again in rows, each full row lighting as a ten with the tens written along the left edge and the part row counted on at the end, and the running count at the top left climbs in tens and then in ones. The child's number stays in the slot the whole time and the count is not compared with it or marked against it.

phases.screen: a ten by ten grid with some cells shaded and both writing slots empty
phases.soWhat: A shaded figure is read by counting the shaded parts for the top number and the total parts for the bottom one.

phases.win: the denominator lands from the lit word and the fraction settles above it
phases.does: picks out the last word, writes the denominator from it, then writes the top number
phases.goal: the last word of a spoken amount names the denominator
phases.says: Listen to the last word. What does that word put underneath?
phases.check: Write thirty-seven thousandths as a decimal fraction, and say which word told you the bottom number.
phases.feels: the last word is not the tail of the sentence, it is the word that says how big the pieces are
phases.hands: Say an amount out loud, slowly, and stop hard on the last word: two hundred five thousandths. Ask the class to write down only the bottom number of the fraction first, before anything else, and to say which word told them. Then let them write the top number. Repeat with an amount ending in hundredths and ask what moved.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is the last word of the amount? Second rung, the phase's: what does that word put underneath? Third rung: the bay is cut to a two word amount and the child writes the bottom box first. The number pad and the fraction key stay open.

wrong.why: ten was the first denominator met and every early figure in the chapter had ten underneath, so ten has become what a bottom number looks like.
wrong.move: writes the number heard over ten, whatever word the amount happened to end on.
wrong.screen: the last word of the spoken amount is lit in the words bay and read out on its own, and the ladder lights the rung that word names. The child's fraction stays written where it was put, the bottom box is opened again beside it, and the amount is said once more with the last word held.

wrong.why: the word hundred is plainly in the phrase and it is the only number word in it that names a size, so it looks like the word that was doing the naming.
wrong.move: hears the word hundred inside two hundred five thousandths and writes a hundred underneath.
wrong.screen: the phrase is laid out word by word along the words bay and the words that build the top number are lit together as one group, with the last word left lit on its own at the end. The child's denominator stays in its box, the two readings are stood one above the other, and the grid and the ladder are asked which of the two sizes of piece is being counted.

phases.screen: an amount said in words, with the words bay open and its last word waiting
phases.soWhat: The last word of a spoken amount names the denominator.
phases.concept: From words straight to a decimal fraction

writeup.delight: The first phase, at the moment the split lands. The piece rides up into the glass and the gap it left along the strip stays open behind it, and the cut runs through it in one movement into ten pieces that are plainly of one size. Drag them back out and they walk down to their real size on the way, and lay themselves along the gap one at a time; the tenth one closes it and the strip is whole again, with the ten small pieces still drawn inside the space of the one they came from. Lift and split the same piece again and it all runs once more, as often as a finger likes, and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the strip lies cut into ten with one piece already lifted into the glass and a plain gap left along the strip where it came from. On the second the hundred grid stands built with one of its cells lifted into the glass and the ladder holding two names with a rung left blank under them. On the third a grid stands with some of its cells shaded and both writing slots empty, the glass parked and the ladder complete. On the fourth an amount said in words lies along the words bay with its last word lit and the two boxes of a fraction drawn empty above it. The running count at the top left holds the splits made against the splits this phase lays out, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the piece in the glass, or the blank rung of the ladder, or the first shaded cell, or the lit last word, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what this piece is going to be called. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any piece lifted, split as often as the stage allows, with the grid, the counting bay and the words bay all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on how many hundredths make a tenth, on the next split down, on reading a shaded grid, and on turning spoken words into a decimal fraction.
voiceLines: One piece off the strip and into the glass. Watch what happens when it is cut again.
Cut that one tenth into ten. How many of these make the tenth again?
Split it once more. What do you think this one will be called?
Count what is shaded. Now count the whole thing. Write both of them.
Listen to the last word. What does that word put underneath?
Another split. Say what the new piece will be called before it is cut.
Free play. Lift any piece, split as often as the stage allows, grid and words bay open.
Put the pieces back beside the one they came from and count them into it again.
Three names on the ladder, and every one of them made by the same single cut.

observations.why: The gap it left was never closed up, so the old piece and the new pieces could be held against each other.
observations.soWhat: A new place is made out of the place before it, and the place before it does not go anywhere.
observations.observe: The tenth kept its place on the strip while the piece cut out of it stood in the glass.

observations.why: The tenth was cut into ten equal pieces, so ten of them are the tenth again.
observations.soWhat: One tenth is ten hundredths, and that is a fact about the cutting rather than a rule to learn.
observations.observe: Ten of the small pieces laid back along the tenth filled it exactly, with none left over.

observations.why: The move that made it was the same move made once more, so the name could be said before it was seen.
observations.soWhat: Every place is a tenth of the place on its left, so the pattern carries on past what a page can draw.
observations.observe: The third name arrived without a thousand pieces ever being drawn.

observations.why: The last word names the size of the pieces being counted, which is what the denominator records.
observations.soWhat: The last word of a spoken amount names the denominator, so it is worth hearing before anything is written.
observations.observe: Changing the last word of the spoken amount changed the bottom number and nothing else.

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: Every tenth of the strip splits the same way and is counted in tens along the strip, and the card shows the fraction.
Phase 2: The whole is counted rung by rung, tenths, hundredths and thousandths, and the third name lands on the ladder from that count.
Phase 3: The shaded rows are counted in tens down the left edge, every row to a hundred down the right, and the cards show the amount.
Phase 4: The last word lights with its rung, the number words light together as the top number, and the fraction lands bottom first.

voice.opening: One piece off the strip and into the glass. Watch what happens when it is cut again.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play: add ten or add one, then read the fraction and the decimal.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs, shown at once UNDER the pinned instruction and kept until the child acts again
voice.onFinish: Three names on the ladder, and every one of them made by the same single cut.
voice.rules: Silent: nothing is spoken (no device speech, no recorded clips, no Tap to start cover). The speech bubble is the guide: every instruction and hint is one printed page, numbers as words. The lesson is action-driven in every mode: a guide step's instruction stays until the child does the act it names; the bubble holds ONE sentence: a wrong act shows that step's hint in place of the instruction, a wrong answer the next rung of its ladder, and the instruction comes back when the child taps again (a key, the card or the Answer key) or does the right act; at a phase's last right answer the bubble shows only the phase's closing line; a right answer's next question, a phase's next phase and the summary's rows follow by themselves after a short celebration. The header's Hint key shows the step's hint or the next rung on demand. What is heard is sound effects (Web Audio), switched by the sound button, on in every mode. In classroom mode nothing waits for a tap except the pieces of a long line (the blinking arrow; a tap, Enter, Space, ArrowRight or PageDown on the bubble shows the next piece), and a tap on the bubble when nothing waits is the teacher's skip.

guide.playsOn: guide steps on phase 1, 2, 3, 4: the phase opens on its first instruction and waits for the child's act (getState guideStep, guideSteps, guideOn); the agent's check() performs the current step; the last act opens the first question. Other phases open on their printed teach lines, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page (a tool with nextKey, runtime r48+: in user mode it waits for the child's blinking Next key instead, after every question and every phase, and the last phase's key opens the summary; AI mode, and a host that mounts one phase without navigableDots, walk on by themselves); finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.

getState: toolId, mediaId, mode, mountPhase, phase, phases, conceptId, objectiveIds, step, steps, item, items, stage (teach, demo, ask, win, idle, summary, free), question, questionText, choices, typed, keypadOpen, tries, answered, firstTry, score, maxScore, answerShown (only after the answer), complete, questionCount, muted (the sound effects), speaking (always false: the lesson is silent), voice ("silent"), mascot, summaryRow, played, classroom, held (a classroom's parked piece of a long line), instruction (the pinned line), hint (the hint under it, or null), guideStep / guideSteps / guideOn (a guide-steps phase only), lifted, splitDepth, complete

terminalEvent.name: finished
terminalEvent.fires: once per mount, from the summary page after the last phase, 5 s after the page opens (its lines may still be going on); one-shot guarded and re-armed by restart or Play again; never sent at the end of an earlier phase (the tool walks on), and never if Free play or Play again is tapped first

sounds: Web Audio, no files, on in every mode (the sound button switches them): correct, wrong (soft), win at a phase end, cheer at the last, a tick when a piece snaps, and cut, settle and trade where the picture moves

voiceLines.en: One piece off the strip and into the glass. Watch what happens when it is cut again.
Cut that one tenth into ten. How many of these make the tenth again?
Split it once more. What do you think this one will be called?
Count what is shaded. Now count the whole thing. Write both of them.
Listen to the last word. What does that word put underneath?
Another split. Say what the new piece will be called before it is cut.
Free play. Lift any piece, split as often as the stage allows, grid and words bay open.
Put the pieces back beside the one they came from and count them into it again.
Three names on the ladder, and every one of them made by the same single cut.
